No third party, works behind NAT, CGNAT and VPN. The server must set REQUIRE_SOURCE_ADDRESS N: the packet is then no longer tied to your IP and only the replay digest protects it. The fwknop documentation advises against it.

Before HTTPS, ask a STUN server (Cloudflare, then Google) over UDP like the knock. Unencrypted.
If HTTPS fails, ask OpenDNS (Cisco) over unencrypted DNS. Many ISPs and Wi-Fi networks redirect it: its answer is checked against the other probes and flagged when they disagree.
Automatic goes through the VPN only for servers it routes (WireGuard split tunnel, Tailscale…) and around it otherwise. Outside the VPN, the server, STUN and HTTPS lookups see your real address.

Single Packet Authorization client for fwknop

FwKnop-ng is a client for fwknop Single Packet Authorization (SPA). Your server keeps its ports closed; tapping Knock sends one encrypted and authenticated UDP packet, and fwknopd then opens the requested ports to your IP for the duration of the timeout.

Enter the server address, the fwknopd port (udp/62201 by default) and the ports to open, e.g. tcp/22. The Rijndael and HMAC keys, their encoding and the digests must match the server\'s access.conf (KEY_BASE64, HMAC_KEY_BASE64). Scan a QR code to fill them in, or leave the key blank to be asked at each knock. GPG keys are handled by OpenKeychain.

By default the app first asks a STUN server, because some carriers hand out addresses that look public but are translated again. It then uses the address the system picks to reach the server, without asking anyone, then the HTTPS address, then OpenDNS if enabled. A local server gets the system address first. These lookups tell the STUN, HTTPS and DNS operators your public address and when you knock: the diagnostic lists those queried. The SPA message only carries an IPv4 address, so the app always knocks the server\'s IPv4 address, even on an IPv6 mobile network. The method used is shown after each knock. The packet source IP mode asks no one and works behind any NAT, but the server must set REQUIRE_SOURCE_ADDRESS N, which fwknop advises against. You can also set a fixed IP.
Keep open re-knocks shortly before the timeout expires. The app can then launch an SSH client (ConnectBot), an OpenVPN profile or a WireGuard tunnel.
A tag only holds a digest, never a key. With NFC knocking and the app lock enabled, holding it against the unlocked app knocks the matching config.
Configs are encrypted on the device. Turn on the app lock in the settings, and use a passphrase-encrypted export to move your configs to another device: Android backups cannot restore them.
If nothing opens, first check the server logs: keys, digests or clock out of sync between phone and server. For a server on your local network, allow “Nearby devices” in the app permissions.

When the device leaves all these networks, the configuration is knocked through the next network (mobile data…), without launching the app linked to it. With the app lock on, this only happens while the app is unlocked. A notification stays visible while the monitoring runs.

The automatic knock sends an SPA packet without any action from you, each time the device leaves a trusted Wi-Fi network.

• The port opens for the public IP of the next network (mobile data, public Wi-Fi…) even if you did not mean to connect. Anyone sharing that address (carrier NAT, hotspot) can reach the service while the rule lasts.

• A lost or stolen phone knocks too. Without the app lock, the configuration key is used without any authentication.

• A network name proves nothing: anyone can broadcast the same SSID and make the phone join and leave it, to trigger knocks.

• The app reads the Wi-Fi network name in the background, which Android ties to the location permission “All the time”. No position is recorded or sent.

• A background service runs permanently.

Keep this for a dedicated configuration with a short open time.
